Package org.aeonbits.owner.loaders

Interface Loader

All Superinterfaces:
Serializable
All Known Implementing Classes:
DotEnvLoader, HoconLoader, IniLoader, JndiLoader, JsonLoader, PropertiesLoader, SystemLoader, TomlLoader, XMLLoader, YamlLoader, ZooKeeperLoader
public interface Loader extends Serializable
Defines the interface of a generic Properties loader.

Getting a loader into a factory

Two ways, and the difference between them is who is being explicit.

Registering it is the explicit way, and it works everywhere: 

     ConfigFactory.registerLoader(new YamlLoader());

Being discovered is the implicit way. A loader listed in META-INF/services/org.aeonbits.owner.loaders.Loader is found by ServiceLoader when a factory is created, which requires it to be a public class with a public no-argument constructor - that is ServiceLoader's rule, not OWNER's. Being discovered enables it: the loader answers for its formats immediately, and its default spec joins the sources looked for when an interface carries no @Sources. That is what Spring Boot, MicroProfile and Gestalt all do.

Which class loader does the looking

The context class loader of the thread creating the factory, falling back on the one that loaded OWNER when there is no context class loader. It is right more often than the alternative, and it is not right always:

  • In an application server, with OWNER in the shared libraries and the loader in a web application's WEB-INF/lib, only the context class loader can see it - a parent never sees a child's jars.
  • On a thread that a container or a pool set up, the context class loader may point somewhere that knows nothing of the application, and the loader is not found although it is on the classpath.
  • Under OSGi there is no class path to search and ServiceLoader needs help from the container to work at all.

In each of those, register the loader explicitly. That path depends on nothing.

What a loader that is not found looks like

Not like an error. PropertiesLoader accepts every URL it can resolve and is consulted last, so a app.yaml whose loader was not discovered is not left unread - it is read as a properties file, and the configuration comes back holding almost nothing, with nothing said. When a format seems to be ignored, org.aeonbits.owner.level = CONFIG makes the library name the loaders it discovered, which tells a loader that is absent from a loader that is broken.

Where a loader sits among the others

A registered loader comes before a discovered one, a discovered one before the built-in loaders, and PropertiesLoader last. For the sources looked for in the absence of @Sources the order is deliberately not the same: a discovered loader comes last there, so that a jar arriving on the classpath cannot make a stray MyConfig.yaml take precedence over the MyConfig.properties an application already loads. Among several discovered loaders the order is the class path's, which is not guaranteed to be the same on two machines: two loaders claiming one format is a situation to avoid rather than to order.

Options on a source

The query belongs to the protocol and the fragment belongs to OWNER. A loader reads what was written on a single source through SourceOptions, and refuses an option it does not recognise rather than ignoring it.

Serialization

A loader is Serializable because a Config object holds the ones that were in force when it was created. A configuration serialized where a loader was present and read back where it is not fails to deserialize; that was already true of a registered loader and discovery makes it likelier.

    • defaultSpecFor

      default String defaultSpecFor(String uriPrefix)
      Returns the default URI specification for a given URI resource, that can be handled by this loader.

      Returning null means this loader adds nothing to the sources looked for in the absence of @Sources - which is what SystemLoader and DotEnvLoader both do, since neither is named after the configuration interface. That is also why this method has a default: it is a choice a loader is allowed to decline, and declining it should not require writing a method that returns nothing.

      A loader offering more than one name - a format spelled .yaml and .yml, or .ini and .cfg - overrides defaultSpecsFor(String) instead. The two are not meant to be overridden together.

      Parameters:
      uriPrefix - the prefix identifying the URI resource.
      Returns:
      the default URI specification for a given URI resource, or null for none.

    • defaultSpecsFor

      default String[] defaultSpecsFor(String uriPrefix)
      Returns every default URI specification this loader offers, and is the one the library calls.

      The default answers with whatever defaultSpecFor(String) returned, so a loader with a single name has nothing to do here and a loader written before this method existed keeps working unchanged. Override this one, and not that one, when a format goes by several names: 

           @Override
     public String[] defaultSpecsFor(String uriPrefix) {
         return new String[] { uriPrefix + ".yaml", uriPrefix + ".yml" };
     }

      The order matters: these are tried in the order given, and under Config.LoadType.FIRST the first one that resolves is the one that answers. An empty array, like a null from the single-valued method, means this loader adds nothing.

      Parameters:
      uriPrefix - the prefix identifying the URI resource.
      Returns:
      the default URI specifications, in the order they should be tried; never containing null.
      Since:
      2.0.0
